tier_reason: Peer-reviewed OSDI'22 paper (draft checked into the artifact repo) compares XRP against read(), io_uring and SPDK on a stated i5-8500 + Optane P5800X setup; build scripts are public but compiler and flags are not stated, so not A.

corrections.claimed_speedup: BPF-KV random 512 B lookups, 3 on-disk index levels, multiple threads: 47%-94% higher throughput and 20%-34% lower p99 latency than read(); B-tree lookup throughput up to 2.5x over normal system calls; WiredTiger up to 24% under YCSB. Motivation study (Figure 3, BPF hook in the NVMe driver with io_uring): up to 1.5x over io_uring for small batches and up to 2.5x as batch size grows (single-threaded).
corrections.caveats: Compiler flags not stated in the paper draft (build scripts not inspected). The io_uring 1.5x/2.5x figures come from the paper's motivation section (Figure 3), not the main XRP evaluation. Closed-loop experiment, so XRP runs at higher throughput than the baselines in latency plots. Prototype limits: 512 B I/O requests, no fanout; requires a modified Linux 5.12 kernel (kernel part is GPL-2.0 kernel code; repo LICENSE is Apache-2.0). Last commit 2022-12-12.

notes: All claimed numbers found in the abstract and section 2 of 'XRP Draft.pdf' (pdftotext). Last commit 2022-12-12 is more than 3 years ago, so maintenance moved to abandoned.

tier_reason: First-party hyperfine run against GNU find and fdfind in the README; benchmark generator (benchmark_scenario.c) and Makefile flags (gcc -Wall -pthread -O3) are public, but no CPU model or filesystem is stated, so not A.

corrections.claimed_speedup: Listing 765,200 entries: find 3.178 s, fdfind -HI 1.633 s, dent 563.9 ms (5.64x faster than find, 2.90x faster than fdfind); with grep for a regex: 6.01x faster than find -iregex, 1.60x faster than fdfind
corrections.caveats: No hardware or filesystem stated; single synthetic scenario (benchmark_scenario.c); warm cache implied; fd and dent are both multithreaded (system time exceeds wall time), find is single-threaded. README says the multithreading was written with ChatGPT. Default MAX_CONCURRENT_THREADS is 1000.

notes: A LICENSE file exists at the repo root and is MIT (Copyright 2024 roy reznik), so usability moves from reference to copyable. Numbers match the README exactly.

tier_reason: First-party numbers from tests/t_compare.py on GitHub Actions runners (Python 3.14) against aiofiles; benchmark code is public but no CPU model or compiler flags, and Windows headline figures are local unspecified NVMe runs.

corrections.claimed_speedup: Linux io_uring random 4 KiB reads vs aiofiles: 191.5K vs 9.8K ops/s at x1 (19.6x), 361.6K vs 10.2K at x16 (35.4x), 361.2K vs 12.5K at x64 (28.9x); small 4 KiB sequential reads 9.2x; macOS 4 KiB sequential read 499K ops/s (27.2x over aiofiles; the README's 6.8K figure is the earlier value, not aiofiles); Windows (local) sequential write 3,046 MB/s at 4 MiB (stated 1.47x over aiofiles)
corrections.caveats: Baseline is aiofiles, a thread-pool wrapper, not POSIX pread or io_uring; reads are cache-hot (macOS small reads complete inline via mincore + pread); hardware and flags not captured; CI runner numbers swing about 2x run to run. Not faster everywhere: aiofiles pulls ahead on Linux 4 MiB sequential writes (0.4x), and the windows-2022 CI run measured 64 KiB sequential read at 0.79x and 4 KiB small reads at 0.62x of aiofiles. README arrow figures (6.8K to 499K, 929 to 3,046 MB/s) mix before/after values with the aiofiles ratio. Python package, only weakly in scope for the C++ filter. Commits are labelled AI-assisted.

notes: Numbers verified in the README Benchmarks section; corrected the macOS phrasing (6.8K is not the aiofiles number since 499/6.8 is about 73x) and documented the cells where it is slower than aiofiles. License MIT, last commit 2026-10-05, 43 stars confirmed.
